## Why Subgroup Analyses Fail






## The PATH Statement - [Kent et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7750907/){style="color: blue;"}

The goal of the PATH statement is to improve reporting of predictive approaches to treatment heterogeneity.

::: {style="margin-top: 2rem; padding: 0.8rem 1.1rem; border: 1px solid #84003d; border-radius: 10px; display: inline-block; background: #ADD8E6; font-size: 0.8em;"}
<ul style="margin: 0; padding-left: 1.2em;">

<li>Treatment effects vary meaningfully across patients with different baseline risks.</li>

<li>Traditional one-variable subgroups often miss important, clinically relevant differences.</li>

<li>PATH combines patient characteristics to estimate more individualized treatment benefit.</li>

</ul>
:::

## Overall outcome of studies

<ul style="margin: 0; padding-left: 1.2em;"> <li><strong>IST:</strong> aspirin reduced death or non-fatal recurrent stroke (OR 0.89).</li>
<li><strong>DIG:</strong> all-cause mortality digoxin versus placebo (RR 0.99).</li> 
<li><strong>GUSTO-I:</strong> 30-day mortality was reduced with accelerated tPA versus with streptokinase (OR 0.85).</li> 
<li><strong>VITAL:</strong> Supplementation with vitamin D did not result in a lower incidence of cancer or cardiovascular events than placebo</li> </ul> 

::: {style="margin-top: 0.8rem; padding: 0.8rem 1rem; border-left: 4px solid #84003d; background: #f8f8f8; font-size: 0.8em;"}
How might the magnitude and direction of the overall treatment effect in each trial influence the ability to detect heterogeneous treatment effects?
:::

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("PATH.png")
```

## Logistic Regression Specification

For each trial, the logistic regression model was specified <em>a priori</em> using domain knowledge from peer-reviewed clinical and methodological papers, with covariates chosen for their prognostic relevance and availability at baseline.

::: {style="margin-top: 1rem; padding: 0.8rem 1rem; border: 1px solid #84003d; border-radius: 10px; background: #ADD8E6; font-size: 0.8em;"}
For the IST trial, the adjustment model was informed by [Thompson et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25497979/). The specification used baseline predictors of 14-day mortality:

$$
\text{logit}\big(P(\text{death14}_i = 1)\big)
=
\beta_0
+ \beta_1 \text{AGE}_i
+ \beta_2 \text{consc}_i \\
\qquad
+ \beta_3 \text{ct\infarct}_i 
+ \beta_4 \text{motor}_i
+ \beta_5 \text{afib}_i
$$
:::

## Random Forest Specification

- The random forest models were fit using all prognostic baseline variables available in each dataset for risk stratification. 
- This flexible strategy was informed by ensemble-learning approaches in the IST trial [Hwangbo et al. 2022](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-22323-9).

::: {style="margin-top: 1rem; padding: 0.8rem 1rem; border: 1px solid #84003d; border-radius: 10px; background: #ADD8E6; font-size: 0.8em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
rf_fit_IST <- ranger(
  death14 ~ AGE + SEX + RCONSC + RSBP + RATRIAL + RDELAY +
    RSLEEP + RCT + RVISINF + RDEF1 + RDEF2 + RDEF3 + RDEF4 + RDEF5,
  data = IST_df,
  probability = TRUE,
  num.trees = 1000,
  seed = 88
)
```
:::

## Simulation Study Design

- **Aim**: Evaluate whether risk-based interaction testing falsely detects treatment effect heterogeneity under the null

- **Data-generating mechanism**  

::: {style="margin-top: 1rem; padding: 0.8rem 1rem; border: 1px solid #84003d; border-radius: 10px; background: #ADD8E6; font-size: 0.8em;"}
$$
\text{logit}\{P(Y_i = 1)\}
=
-2 -0.5Z_i + X_i\beta
$$

$$
X_j \sim N(0,1),
\qquad
Z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.5)
$$
:::

#
- **Estimand / Target**  
$$
H_0:\beta_{Z \times lp}=0
$$


- **Methods**: Risk modelling + likelihood ratio interaction testing

- **Performance measure**: Empirical rejection rate at $\alpha = 0.05$
